Lighthouse mobile >= 90 as deploy blockers. Measured on 2026-08-07 against
a production build, the site does not meet three of them:
metric                 §22 target   measured   closes in
LCP (mobile, 4x CPU)   <= 2000ms    2603-2816  W2-W6   (best-of-3, varies)
initial JS (gzip)      <= 184320    191392     W2 (hero) / W7 (app shell)
best-practices          >= 0.95      0.93       W9
These are structural, not regressions W0 introduced.
WHAT DOMINATES LCP, measured rather than assumed (2026-08-08, production
build, 390x844 at 4x CPU throttle, PerformanceObserver on the live page):
TTFB                        13 ms      (5 samples: 9-17 ms)
stylesheets complete        91 ms      (47.5 KB across 5 files)
first paint                204 ms
first contentful paint     808 ms
LCP                        808 ms      element: <h1>, not an image
An earlier revision of this comment said LCP was dominated by TTFB, and
that force-dynamic in layout.tsx - a consequence of the per-request CSP
nonce in src/proxy.ts - was therefore the thing to fix. That is wrong, and
wrong in an expensive direction: acting on it means weakening a CSP on a
security product to buy 13 ms. TTFB is not the problem and the nonce is
not the problem.
The LCP element is the h1. It is present in the server HTML at 27 ms, has
opacity 1, no animation, and its font is configured display:swap with a
metric-matched fallback - so nothing about the text or the typeface delays
it. The ~700 ms between stylesheets being ready and the h1 painting is
main-thread work: parsing and evaluating the initial JS. That is the same
191 KB the budget above already flags, and it is the legacy marketing page
plus the client AppShell, both of which V3 replaces wholesale in W2 and W7.
So the three misses have one cause between them, and it is already
scheduled. The hero poster (22.8 KB AVIF at 390px) is not implicated - it
is not even the LCP element.
Rather than relax the budget to make the job green - which is how §22
became a declaration in the first place - the assertions below are a
RATCHET. Nothing may get worse, and each wave that rebuilds a scene should
lower these numbers toward §22.
LCP is 2900, and that number has a history worth keeping. lhci asserts on
the optimistic value across three runs, and on shared runners that value
itself moves: 2603, 2726, 2816 have all been observed as the minimum, with
individual samples reaching 3218. A threshold inside that band fails at
random, and a gate that fails at random is one people learn to ignore -
which is worse than no gate. It was set at 2700 twice and flapped twice.
The rule for changing it: raise it ONLY with the measurements that show
the band moved and a statement of why the code did not cause it. Never
raise it to make a build pass. Lowering it needs no justification.
ONE AUDIT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: errors-in-console. Lighthouse counts a
failed network request as a console error, and the Next.js App Router
prefetches every <Link> in view then aborts those requests on teardown -
24 ERR_ABORTED on ?_rsc= URLs per run. Measured against a production build
on 2026-08-07: 0 console errors, 0 page errors, 0 responses >= 400, and 0
failed requests that were not an RSC prefetch. The audit cannot tell the
framework's behaviour from an application defect, so the precise check
lives in e2e/evidence.spec.ts instead, which filters to real console
errors and pageerrors and asserts zero. Do not re-add this audit here
without also removing the reason it fires.
